strengths: Clinically Grounded Trajectory Synthesis: The framework introduces a thoughtful multi-type trajectory construction method (Types 1, 2, and 3) that integrates disease taxonomy trees and differential diagnosis (DDx) graphs to model realistic clinical reasoning, including reflective error correction.

Well-Designed Hierarchical RL Framework: The paper effectively addresses data heterogeneity and sparse annotations by formulating a multi-tier reward system (granularity-wise reward based on taxonomy depth, malignancy discrimination, and structural format compliance) within Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Insightful SFT vs. RL Analysis: The ablation studies empirically demonstrate an important finding: relying solely on RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) without high-quality grounded SFT leads to suboptimal performance in medical VLM reasoning, underscoring the critical role of cold-start expert rationales.

Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: The method is rigorously evaluated across six in-distribution dermatology datasets and five out-of-distribution benchmarks from OmniMedVQA, demonstrating consistent and clear gains in both disease diagnosis accuracy and balanced lesion condition classification (F1).
weaknesses: Lack of Quantitative Evaluation for Reasoning Rationales: While the paper emphasizes 'trustworthy clinical reasoning' and provides qualitative case examples, the evaluation relies predominantly on multiple-choice question (MCQ) accuracy and F1. A formal quantitative evaluation (such as an expert dermatologist study assessing rationale faithfulness, clinical correctness, or hallucination rates) would significantly strengthen the claims.

Details on Synthetic Dataset Scale and Quality Control: The main text leaves out details regarding the exact size of the synthesized SkinRationale dataset (number of images, distribution across classes) and whether any expert clinical filtering was performed to verify the LLM-generated rationales.

Minor Writing and Presentation Polish: There are minor typos and formatting issues in the manuscript (e.g., 'Ambiguit of differential diagnosis' on page 4, 'Balances It balances' on page 19, and entirely empty entries '-' for SkinVL-PubMM in Table 2 without explicit quantification of parsing failures).

strengths: Clinically Grounded Post-Training Formulation: Dermatology diagnosis inherently relies on differential diagnosis (DDx) and taxonomic hierarchies. The proposed framework directly targets these domain-specific characteristics by designing three distinct diagnostic trajectory types (direct mapping, DDx without revision, and DDx with reflective revision) and hierarchical reward signals.

Sound Technical Framework: Combining textbook-guided cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) addresses the instability and superficial reasoning often seen in pure RLVR/RL-from-scratch setups in specialized medical domains.

Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation: The paper evaluates the model across six diverse dermatology benchmarks for in-distribution testing, plus five external subsets from OmniMedVQA for out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. The proposed Skin-R1 consistently outperforms both general VLMs and medical-specialized VLMs by substantial margins.

Insightful Ablation and Targeted Benchmarks: The ablation studies clearly demonstrate that trajectory SFT is crucial before running GRPO (countering recent trends that bypass SFT for pure RL). Furthermore, the targeted hierarchical and DDx stress tests (Section 4.3) provide compelling evidence for the specific mechanisms introduced.
weaknesses: Lack of Human Expert Evaluation on Rationales: While the paper claims to advance 'trustworthy clinical reasoning,' all primary evaluations are automated multiple-choice accuracy and F1 scores. The paper lacks a systematic, blinded qualitative review by certified board dermatologists assessing the faithfulness, hallucination rate, and clinical soundness of the generated rationales.

Evaluation Confined to Multiple-Choice VQA: Multiple-choice QA can introduce spurious elimination shortcuts. Evaluating the framework on open-ended diagnostic generation or free-text clinical report synthesis would provide stronger evidence of clinical utility.

Details on Dataset Provenance and Scale: Key details regarding the textbook extraction process (e.g., specific reference sources, licensing/copyright status, exact count of extracted images and cases in the SkinRationale dataset) are insufficiently documented in the main text.

Minor Writing and Proofreading Glitches: The text contains several typographical oversights, such as duplicated words (e.g., 'Balances It balances' on page 19) and incomplete sentences in qualitative examples (e.g., '...there is no mention of the Therefore...' on page 20).

strengths: Clinically grounded motivation: Formulating dermatological diagnosis using structured disease taxonomies and differential diagnosis (DDx) reflects real-world clinical decision pathways rather than treating skin disease diagnosis as a flat classification task.

Well-structured trajectory generation framework: The paper details a clear procedural pipeline for synthesizing three trajectory types (direct mapping, non-revision DDx, and reflective revision DDx) with explicit fallback mechanisms.

Hierarchically-aware RL reward design: Incorporating taxonomy depth ($R_{\text{gran}}$) and malignancy status ($R_{\text{malignancy}}$) into the GRPO objective offers an effective task-specific adaptation of verifiable reinforcement learning.

Thorough ablation of the training stages: The ablation experiments effectively demonstrate the complementary nature of SFT trajectory initialization and subsequent RL optimization, showing that direct RL from the base model leads to suboptimal convergence.
weaknesses: Lack of expert clinical evaluation on reasoning quality: Despite the title focusing on 'trustworthy clinical reasoning' and claims of mitigating diagnostic hallucinations, the empirical evaluation is almost entirely restricted to multiple-choice final diagnostic accuracy and Macro F1. There is no quantitative clinical evaluation (e.g., dermatologist-graded rubric or expert rating) assessing the clinical correctness, evidence grounding, and visual faithfulness of the generated rationales.

Potentially unfair baseline comparisons: The baselines appear significantly hindered by format mismatch and instruction-following failures under the rigid multiple-choice format. For instance, the authors note that SkinVL-PubMM failed to generate valid answers (resulting in complete absence in Table 2) and MedGemma exhibited extreme option collapse. Comparing an RL-fine-tuned model trained specifically on the target tag format against off-the-shelf zero-shot models without equivalent task adaptation/in-context prompting inflates the reported performance gap.

Missing specifics on textbook dataset curation and potential contamination: Section 3.1 and Appendix B lack concrete statistics on the size, disease distribution, and specific textbook sources used to build the SkinRationale dataset. Furthermore, dermatological textbooks frequently reuse clinical images from public repositories (such as ISIC, HAM10000, or DermNet); the paper does not clarify whether strict image de-duplication was performed to prevent test-set contamination during the SFT trajectory generation.

Writing and editorial polish: Several typos and grammatical oversights are present in the text (e.g., 'as a warm for large-scale RL training' on p. 2, 'Ambiguit of differential diagnosis' on p. 4, 'achievs' on p. 8, and 'Balances It balances' on p. 19).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in medical vision-language modeling: combining structured, authoritative clinical knowledge (disease taxonomy and differential diagnosis) with reinforcement learning to avoid hallucination and shortcut learning.

Well-motivated trajectory synthesis pipeline: The generation of three distinct types of diagnostic trajectories (direct, contrastive DDx without revision, and reflective DDx revision) provides clinically structured supervision for the cold-start SFT stage.

Principled reward formulation in GRPO: Incorporating normalized depth on the hierarchical disease taxonomy into the reward function directly aligns the optimization objective with diagnostic granularity and clinical categorization.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Extensive evaluation across six dermatology datasets and an out-of-distribution benchmark (OmniMedVQA), outperforming both general-purpose and specialized medical VLMs, even surpassing several larger models (e.g., 32B).

Detailed ablations and transparent qualitative examples: The ablations convincingly demonstrate that cold-start trajectory SFT provides a crucial foundation that pure RL cannot match, and that hierarchical rewards boost out-of-distribution generalization.
weaknesses: Evaluation primarily relies on multiple-choice VQA: While standardized multiple-choice testing is suitable for reproducible benchmarking, clinical reasoning is open-ended. The intermediate reasoning chains and rationale faithfulness are only evaluated qualitatively rather than quantitatively (e.g., via blinded clinician ratings or automated clinical concept alignment metrics).

Coupling of the evaluation distractor generation with the learned taxonomy: For the in-distribution and targeted DDx benchmarks, options and distractors are constructed using the same DDx graph and taxonomy structure as used during training design, which may give an inherent structural advantage over baseline models.

Single backbone exploration: The framework is demonstrated only on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Evaluating whether this SFT+RL recipe consistently transfers across other backbones (e.g., InternVL or LLaVA architectures) would strengthen the generality of the findings.

strengths: Sound clinical motivation: Dermatological diagnosis naturally relies on hierarchical taxonomies and differential diagnosis (DDx). Grounding both the initial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trajectories and the reinforcement learning (RL) reward design in disease taxonomies is methodologically well-conceived and clinically relevant.

Effective two-stage training paradigm: The combination of a high-quality, textbook-derived cold-start (SkinRationale) followed by taxonomy-guided GRPO effectively addresses common pitfalls of pure RL (e.g., shortcut learning and hallucinated reasoning paths) in medical domains, as demonstrated by the ablations.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The framework is benchmarked across six diverse dermatology datasets for in-distribution diagnosis, evaluates lesion condition classification, and tests out-of-distribution generalization on OmniMedVQA. Skin-R1 shows consistent, substantial gains over general-purpose and specialized medical VLMs.

Thorough ablations and honest discussion: The ablation experiments effectively isolate the contribution of each component (SFT initialization, RL training steps, granularity-wise reward vs. standard reward). The authors also provide a frank discussion of limitations, including evaluation of performance across Fitzpatrick skin types.
weaknesses: Outcome-only RL reward without process supervision: Although SFT teaches reasoning trajectories, the GRPO reward function (Eq. 6–9) rewards only format compliance, taxonomy depth of the predicted label, and malignancy classification. Because the intermediate reasoning trace is not rewarded or verified during RL, the policy could still develop ungrounded rationales or post-hoc justifications during test-time generation.

Coupling between knowledge base and evaluation distractors: For the in-distribution and targeted DDx benchmarks, multiple-choice distractors are generated using the same taxonomy ($T_{tax}$) and DDx graph ($G_{DDx}$) used to formulate the training strategy. While the out-of-distribution benchmark (OmniMedVQA) mitigates this concern, this coupling may give Skin-R1 an inherent structural advantage on in-distribution tasks.

Limited scale and single source of textbook grounding: SkinRationale is derived from a single textbook source (Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, Neoplasia section), starting from only 220 base diagnostic exemplars expanded to 2,020 synthetic trajectories via GPT-4o-mini. The scope of dermatological conditions and potential LLM synthesis artifacts remain bounded by this extraction pipeline.

Exploration across model backbones: The entire pipeline is demonstrated exclusively on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Demonstrating the transferability of the SFT+RL recipe to other base models (e.g., InternVL or medical foundation models) would further validate its generality.

strengths: Clinically Grounded Problem Formulation: Integrating hierarchical disease taxonomy and differential diagnosis (DDx) into vision-language reasoning aligns well with real-world dermatological practice, directly targeting known failure modes of general VLMs in medical diagnosis.

Structured Trajectory Construction: The synthesis of three complementary trajectory types (direct diagnostic mapping, DDx without revision, and reflective DDx revision) provides a structured and principled cold-start initialization for supervised fine-tuning.

Hierarchical Reward Formulation: Incorporating normalized depth within the disease taxonomy into the GRPO reward function ($R_{\text{gran}}$) provides meaningful partial credit and guidance compared to flat, binary reward formulations.

Extensive Empirical Benchmarking: The paper evaluates the model across 6 in-distribution datasets and 5 out-of-distribution datasets (from OmniMedVQA), demonstrating consistent gains over strong general and medical VLM baselines, complemented by informative ablation studies.
weaknesses: Lack of Quantitative Evaluation on Reasoning Trace Faithfulness: The RL phase relies entirely on outcome-level rewards (multiple-choice answer correctness and format compliance). Because intermediate reasoning traces ($CoT$) receive no explicit process-level reward or clinical verification, the paper does not quantitatively verify whether the generated rationales remain clinically faithful, unhallucinated, and logically sound after 1,500 RL steps.

Evaluation-Taxonomy Coupling for In-Distribution Benchmarks: For ID benchmarks, multiple-choice distractors are sampled directly from the constructed global taxonomy and DDx graph ($T_{\text{tax}}$ and $G_{\text{DDx}}$). Because the model was explicitly trained with these exact structural relationships during SFT and RL, the reported ID advantages may partially reflect structural overfitting to the curated ontology rather than purely improved visual-clinical reasoning.

Limited Scope and Volume of Textbook Exemplars: The textbook grounding is based on only 220 diagnostic exemplars extracted from a single section (Part 20: Neoplasia) of Fitzpatrick's Dermatology. Although augmented to 2,020 trajectories, this restricts the grounded reasoning distribution heavily toward cutaneous neoplasms, limiting its clinical representativeness for inflammatory, infectious, and rare dermatological conditions.

Absence of Controlled Fine-Tuning Baselines: All baseline comparisons are performed against off-the-shelf general or medical foundation models. To rigorously isolate the specific benefit of the textbook-derived DDx trajectories and hierarchical reward, the authors should include a standard SFT / SFT+RL baseline trained on the exact same image set using conventional classification objectives without DDx trajectory framing.
